**Verdict:** He'd almost certainly tell you not to. To him an MLM is the shortcut he says keeps poor people poor, and it puts you at the bottom of his pay ladder: someone else owns the product and the terms, and controls the money.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault never mentions MLMs. I searched the wiki and raw transcripts for "MLM", "multi-level", "network marketing", "pyramid scheme", "downline", Herbalife and Amway, and found nothing. The answer is worked out from his rules on wealth paths, risk and deal structure.

**How we get there**
1. **It's a shortcut, not one of his four paths.** He says wealth comes from picking one of four paths and playing it for a decade: bootstrap your own business, raise capital, invest, or manage a fund. "Poor people stay poor because they want a fast way to get rich." ([yt-sL16tsGafcQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ&t=0s) @ 0:00). An MLM pitched as a way to build wealth is the kind of shortcut he means. You don't own the business, and you aren't investing in one.
2. **It's near the bottom of his pyramid.** He ranks six ways to get paid, and the top ones mean getting "paid first," "no matter what," by whoever controls "the money flow." He gives franchisors and payment processors as examples ([yt-rMJIOK_FgJk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rMJIOK_FgJk&t=758s) @ 12:38, 14:15). In an MLM the company sits in that spot. You get a commission only after you sell, on terms they set and can change. He prefers a revenue share to a profit share because the other side "can play around their profit" (@ 12:38). An MLM compensation plan has that same weakness.
3. **It's risk with no upside you control.** His central rule is that "you will be compensated in proportion to the risk you're willing to take" (@ 7:43). The best bets look risky to others but aren't risky for you, because you're skilled at them (@ 8:16). In an MLM you carry the risk (inventory, buy-ins, your own time) while the company keeps the leverage. That's the reverse of the bet he wants.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Sell what people already pay for.** "research a skill that people already pay money for" ([yt-jfW6gL6hKhk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=420s) @ 7:00), and "the best way to look is not to risk it on something that you don't know, but find stuff people are already spending money on" (@ 14:09). His recommended first move is a skill you own, sold one-on-one, under the 1-1-1 rule: one product, one avatar, one channel until $1M.
- **Bootstrap to pay off ignorance debt, and keep control.** "the main advantage of this is that you keep the control and the equity" ([yt-sL16tsGafcQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ&t=225s) @ 3:45). An MLM gives you neither.
- **Leverage decides your terms.** "the more leverage you have, the further up this pyramid you can go because you can ultimately command your own terms" ([yt-rMJIOK_FgJk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rMJIOK_FgJk&t=197s) @ 3:17). An MLM distributor has almost none.

**What he'd salvage:** the sales reps. He treats sales as the base skill and says to do high volume and shadow the best. If you're already in an MLM, he'd probably say the selling practice is the only part that carries over, so take it and sell your own offer.

**What he's done:** He took the position MLM companies take. He licensed his gym system to other operators (Gym Launch) and sold his supplements, Prestige Labs, through that gym-owner base. He set the terms and controlled the product.

**What would change his answer:** if the "MLM" were really a business you own that sells a product people already pay for, and you set the terms and collect first. At that point it's a bootstrapped distribution business, not an MLM. The inference would also break if he has said something about MLMs that isn't in the vault. It could be worth adding a source where he addresses them directly.

**Verdict:** No. Hormozi would not buy a Lamborghini with his first $1M in profit. His rule is to be rich, not look rich: keep living cheaply, drive a cheap car you own outright, and put the cash back into growth.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: high). He has never talked about buying a Lambo at the $1M mark. But he has given his own view on status cars directly, and he repeats the frugality rule in two sources a year apart.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest thing he's said.** While talking about status in marketing copy, he says a Lamborghini pitch might win over "a hustle bro who's 20 years old". Then he says what he wants for himself: "having cash cars that you can buy for seven grand and then not have to worry about car payment so you can actually rich in your bank account rather than in other people's eyes" ([yt-JDR-R--4HhM @ 20:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=1231s), 2025-05). He was already very rich when he said this, so it isn't advice he only gives to broke beginners.
2. **The rule behind it.** "You want to be rich, not look rich." / "Number six, do not increase your lifestyle." ([yt-jfW6gL6hKhk @ 13:04–13:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=784s), 2026-03). On cars in particular: "ideally a paid-off clunker is the best way to go." (@ 2:08)
3. **Why it applies at $1M.** A Lambo is the textbook example of looking rich and inflating your lifestyle. At $1M of profit you're right where his 1-1-1 rule ends ("sell one product or service to one avatar on one channel until you make $1 million", @ 8:09). That's the moment he'd want the money put to work, not spent on a car.

**Why he'd say it**
- Spare cash is what lets you take risks: "you get rewarded for the risk you take on. You cannot take any risk on if you have no time and no money." (@ 13:04). Money spent on a car can't fund the next location, more ads or more learning.
- He thinks wealth comes from reinvesting what you earn: "most billionaires who are self-made made their money from making money." (@ 12:30)
- He felt richest at $100K in the bank, not after his exits. What he valued was not having to worry about money, not having things (@ 0:00).

**What he's done**
- His first gym paid him about $20K a month, and he kept paying around $400 a month to share a bedroom. He saved the rest for a new location, learning and conferences (@ 1:37, 13:37).

**What would change his answer**
- He tells "big baller" business owners they can skip the frugality roadmap (@ 0:32). So once he's very wealthy and a Lambo would cost him a tiny share of his net worth, he might stop objecting. Even then, the vault only has him choosing cash cars for himself.
- If the car were a marketing expense, he might buy it. Say your audience really is 20-year-old hustle bros and the Lambo brings in more sales than it costs. Then it's a business decision, not lifestyle spending. That's my extrapolation, not something he said.

**Verdict:** Hormozi would probably tell this founder to drop the free-forever plan. His advice is to start with a high price and work down. A free tier attracts the users who value the product least, adds nothing to revenue per customer, and lowers buyers' belief that the product works. If the founder wants something free, he'd make it the marketing (content, or a limited trial) and keep the product itself paid.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has nothing from him on free plans or freemium SaaS specifically. There's also no `thinking/` page, so this applies his pricing and retention rules from the leaves.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest case:** at Skool, cancellations citing price led to a cheaper tier, from $99 down to $9. That's still a paid floor, not $0, and his rule is that only ideal customers' price complaints count: "If non-ideal people say it's too expensive, just ignore it. That means that the price is actually acting as a good filter" ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 8:46, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=526s).
2. **The rule behind it:** start expensive and move down only when evidence says to. "It is significantly easier when you're starting to sell extremely expensive to a select few... you have to make enough money to be able to serve the masses" ([[yt-uWdIgftpvBI]] @ 0:32, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=32s). He also says "the idea is that you start high and then you can work your way down" (@ 1:06).
3. **Applying it:** a free-forever plan is the opposite. It starts at the bottom, removes the price filter completely, and brings in users who'd never pay. It fails all three of his tests: it doesn't fund growth, it doesn't filter for good customers, and it doesn't make more money from each customer.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Price raises belief.** "If you raise your price, you increase the emotional investment, you increase the perceived value, you increase the results, and you decrease the demandingness of the customer" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 7:33, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=453s). By that logic, free users are the least committed and the most demanding. He also warns about founders "so afraid of charging money that they actually sell themselves out of a sale" (same video).
- **The economics have to work.** "All businesses have the cost of getting customers and what you make from those customers as the core economic arbitrage" ([[yt-uWdIgftpvBI]] @ 0:00). His fix for expensive customer acquisition is to "make more from each one" ([[yt-tGhe3sBuk34]] @ 8:50, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=530s). Free users pay nothing back toward what it costs to get them.
- **Commitment cuts churn.** Annual buyers churn less because "they're also more qualified because they've paid more up front" ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 15:52). He pushes for more money up front, not less.

**What he does himself:** he does give a lot away. His content has "no pay walls" and his books cost 99 cents, but he says openly that this brings deal flow to Acquisition.com: "provide more value to a company before they've ever spoken to us" ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 2:52, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=172s). Skool's free access is a time-limited 30-day trial bundled with his books ([[yt-jfW6gL6hKhk]]). In both cases the free part is marketing that leads to a paid offer.

**What would change his answer:** two things.
- He allows "sell something super cheap to everyone" as a valid strategy ([[yt-uWdIgftpvBI]] @ 0:00). If free users clearly turn into paying ideal customers, the free plan works like his free content. He'd want to see that conversion data, though, not assume it.
- If the paying customers who leave are ideal customers citing price, he'd add a cheaper paid tier, not a free one.

**Caveats:**
- He's involved with Skool, a paid SaaS that avoids a free tier, so he has a stake in this view.
- My own view: freemium does work for some products, like ones that spread through users or have near-zero cost per user. The vault has nothing from him on that kind of case.

Short answer: he'd probably hire them, but only for the same reason he'd hire anyone, which is that they're good at the job and accept his standards up front. Being his best friend wouldn't count in their favour. **The vault never addresses this question**, so this is my inference from what he's said and done nearby.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: low to medium). The vault has no thinking page for him, so I worked from the closest leaves and raw transcripts.

**How I got there**
1. **The closest case is the person nearest to him, and he hired her for her ability.** On his first date with Leila, now his wife, he "pitched her on working for me I was like quit your job work for me… she was a a personal trainer I had a bunch of gyms and I was like if you're this good you…" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 17:29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1049s)). Being close to someone didn't put him off hiring them. What decided it was "if you're this good."
2. **His hiring rule is to screen on fit and set expectations hard.** "these are the values we have here examples of those values" and "if your shift ends at 5 and somebody asks a question that's going to take 30 minutes to answer at 459 what do you do that's an interview question" ([@ 1:16:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4568s)). Anyone who doesn't share that view "shouldn't work here" ([@ 1:16:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4600s)). A best friend would face the same filter.
3. **A friendship is the kind of relationship that hides the truth from you.** "people want to protect your feelings, your friends, your family, they don't want you to feel bad. The market does not care" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=960s), just before 16:13). The danger is that neither of you would say the hard thing, and he'd struggle to fire a friend who isn't performing.
4. **He's already been burned by trusting a relationship over evidence.** He went into a gym deal with a partner even though "he'd already been indicted for fraud um and I knew this," and lost all his money ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 19:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1146s)). That points toward judging people on their record, not on how much he likes them.

**What I think he'd say:** hire the friend only if you'd hire them as a stranger. Run the same values screen and the 4:59 question, and agree in advance that you'll fire them if they don't perform. If you can't picture firing them, don't hire them.

**One thing in the friend's favour:** he cites data that "if an employee has a friend that they are friends with outside of work, they stay five times longer at their job" ([yt--j8_YCWZ05Q @ 16:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=1018s)). That's about friendships among coworkers, not between the owner and an employee, so it's only a loose fit here.

**What would change the answer:** if the friend lacks the skills the business needs right now, he'd almost certainly say no.

**Verdict:** He'd most likely tell the gym owner to stop giving the first month away and charge from day one. If the point is to get people in, he'd say build an offer that's worth paying for, with a fast early win, and add a discounted annual plan.

His reasoning: a higher price makes customers more committed and more likely to get results. Month one is when most members cancel anyway, so a free month fills the gym with people who haven't committed to anything, right when they're most likely to leave.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). He never talks about "first month free" in this vault, but his statements on pricing, churn and offers point clearly one way. (The vault has no `thinking/hormozi` page yet, so this is reasoned from the leaves.)

**How we get there**
1. **Price builds commitment.** "if you raise your price, you increase the emotional investment, you increase the perceived value, you increase the results, and you decrease the demandingness of the customer." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 7:33, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=453s)) He also says owners are "so afraid of charging money that they actually sell themselves out of a sale" (@ 7:33). A free month is a $0 price, which is the far end of what he's warning about.
2. **Month one is where members leave.** "have a very specific strategy for getting people past the first month cuz that's the biggest month of churn" ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 4:57, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=297s)). A free first month puts the first payment exactly where churn is highest, so the "trial" ends just as people are most likely to drop out.
3. **Fix the offer, not the price.** "if we can't get enough people to say yes we need to make the offer better" ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:25:23, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5123s)). He'd read the need for a free month as a sign the offer is weak.

**What he'd tell them to do instead**
- **Get members an early win.** "pin the fast win up front so new members hit that value ideally within the first 24 hours" ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 13:06). Make the first month worth paying for instead of free.
- **Collect cash up front.** He describes money models as a way to "pull cash forward accelerate cash conversion" ([[yt-tGhe3sBuk34]] @ 8:17, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s)). He also says to add a discounted annual plan "like today", because annual buyers are "more qualified because they've paid more up front" ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 15:52). A discount for committing for a year does the opposite of a free month.
- **Use price as a filter.** "If non-ideal people say it's too expensive, just ignore it. That means that the price is actually acting as a good filter" ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 8:46).

**What he's done:** He built Gym Launch on selling gym memberships and ran about six gyms of his own ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]]). The vault doesn't record how those gyms priced the first month, though.

**What would change his answer:**
- **His own free trials.** He does use free trials himself: his book bundle comes with a 30-day Skool trial "so you actually use the stuff" ([[yt-jfW6gL6hKhk]]). So he isn't against trials outright. He'd probably accept a free period if it's attached to something people paid for, or if it leads straight into an upsell.
- **Unit economics.** If the gym's numbers showed free-month members staying past day 90 at a good rate, he'd go with the numbers. He decides by what the data shows, not by rules like this one.
- **Outside the vault.** In his books he's known for gym "challenge" offers where members pay up front and earn money back. The vault doesn't contain that, so I didn't use it as evidence.

**Verdict:** He'd tell you not to do it. Wanting a fast way to get rich is, in his words, what keeps poor people poor. Your savings are meant to be your safety net and the money you put at risk on building a skill people pay for, not on a bet in markets you don't understand yet.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium-high). The vault has nothing on crypto or day trading by name. Several of his stated rules apply directly, though, and they all point the same way.

**How we get there**
1. **The closest thing he said:** in his talk on paths to wealth, his first line is "Poor people stay poor because they want a fast way to get rich. And instead, the richest people that I know pick one of these four paths, play it for a decade" ([yt-sL16tsGafcQ @ 0:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ&t=0s)). A day-trading course is sold as a shortcut.
2. **Trading is his "investing" path, and he says it comes last.** On investing your own money: "this is by far the slowest, number one. And number two, almost no one makes their money this way. They have already have a high active income and then they begin investing." ([@ 14:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ&t=852s)). He only thinks it makes sense "once you have meaningful excess cash" ([@ 13:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ&t=786s)). Your savings don't count as excess cash.
3. **He says your savings are there to give you security.** "The moment that I felt the wealthiest in my entire life was when I had $100,000 in my bank account", because that was when "I stopped having to worry about tomorrow" ([yt-jfW6gL6hKhk @ 0:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=0s)).
4. **He'd tell you to bet on things you know.** "The best way to look is not to risk it on something that you don't know, but find stuff people are already spending money on." ([yt-jfW6gL6hKhk @ 14:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=849s)). His advice is to "research a skill that people already pay money for" ([@ 7:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=420s)). Nobody pays you for day trading. You're on the other side of the market.

**Why he wouldn't just say "never buy courses"**
- He's openly in favour of paying to learn: "the day that you stop spending money on learning is the day you decide that you do not want to make more." ([@ 14:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=849s)). He'd ask *what* the course teaches. He'd back paying for a sellable skill like sales, ads or content, especially one-on-one help. A trading course doesn't fit that.
- He does like risk: "you will be compensated in proportion to the risk you're willing to take" ([yt-rMJIOK_FgJk @ 7:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rMJIOK_FgJk&t=463s)). But the bets he likes are ones that "have it be very risky for other people and not risky at all for them" ([@ 8:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rMJIOK_FgJk&t=496s)). Day trading as a beginner is the reverse: it's riskier for you than it looks.
- On copying star investors: "I wouldn't say, oh, let me look at what the top person in this field did if you're not that person." ([yt-sL16tsGafcQ @ 14:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ&t=885s)). That fits a guru selling a course on how they trade.

**What he's done:** when his first gym paid him about $20K a month, he kept paying about $400 a month in rent. He spent the savings on opening a new location, on learning and on conferences, all going back into the business he ran ([yt-jfW6gL6hKhk @ 13:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=817s)).

**What would change his answer:** having real spare cash on top of a high income from something you actively do, and a very long time horizon. Then putting some money into markets fits his investing path. The weak spot in this inference is that he never actually talks about trading, as opposed to long-term investing. He also prefers concentrated bets to spreading money around (@ 13:38), so he isn't against risk in general. Even so, his rules point against putting your *savings* into a *course* about *short-term* trading.

Caveat from the vault: he earns money from selling education himself (Skool and his book bundles), so his "spend on learning" advice comes with a conflict of interest.

**Verdict:** Probably not. Hormozi wouldn't push a 4-day week on a 10-person agency, and the vault suggests he'd lean against it. He doesn't argue there's one right schedule. His point is that an agency sells its people's time, so if you cut a day you've probably cut what you can deliver. Whatever you choose, he'd want you to say plainly what you expect and hire people who want that.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). Nothing in the vault mentions a 4-day week; I searched both the wiki and the raw transcripts. This is inferred from what he says about work hours, team culture and finding what limits a business.

**How we get there**
1. **The closest thing he's said about staff hours.** At his companies, an interview question tests whether people stretch past the end of a shift: "if your shift ends at 5 and somebody asks a question that's going to take 30 minutes to answer at 459 what do you do that's an interview question" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:16:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4568s)). Shorter hours as a perk is the opposite of what that question screens for.
2. **The rule behind it.** He doesn't say his way is the only way: "I just hardcore reject there is a right way to do things" (@ 1:17:13). What he does insist on is "expectation setting and being very truthful and as transparent as humanly possible about like this is what we expect" (@ 1:16:40). People who disagree "shouldn't work here because there's... another company that totally shares your worldview" (@ 1:16:40).
3. **Applying his first question to an agency.** He always starts with "is this a supply constraint business or a demand constraint business" ([yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4 @ 3:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=227s)). He also warns that owners "fix a problem that if you fix it, makes your existing problem worse" (@ 4:19). Agencies often run short on staff time, and a 4-day week takes about 20% of it away. Unless output per person goes up to make up the difference, that hits the exact thing that limits growth.

**Why he'd say it**
- He likes intense work himself: "I work until I can't work meaning like my put per unit of time starts to drop precipitously" (@ 1:09:28). For people under 30 with no responsibilities: "I recommend working as many hours per week as humanly possible because you will never be able to work this hard again" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 11:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=712s)).
- He respects other people's choices: "the same degree they cannot work at all doesn't affect me" (@ 1:10:32). That's why it's a lean against the 4-day week, not a ban.
- When a team is overwhelmed, his fix is to cut down what you work on, not the hours: "if you do one thing, you also need to have way fewer meetings about it" ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 12:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=760s)). He also says "I promise your team's 10 times more overwhelmed" (@ 13:14).

**What would change his answer:** if clients don't buy your hours (you sell a fixed result) and the agency can't win enough clients rather than lacking staff time, a 4-day week costs little. In that case he'd likely treat it as a perk that helps you hire, as long as you're upfront about it when hiring. A caveat on the evidence: the 2025 "work as many hours as possible" advice was about individuals under 30, not company policy. The vault's tensions page notes he moved from "there is no should" (2023) to recommending specific hours (2025).

**Verdict:** Hormozi would tell this coach they are spread too thin. They should cut down to one product, sold to one avatar on one channel, until it makes $1M, and drop the other 11 or park them.

His reasoning: you can't go deep on 12 things, and the big returns only come to whoever is best at one thing. Offering everything usually means the coach is afraid to choose. Each extra product also takes time and money away from the one that would have worked.

**Based on:** he has said this directly about products and SKUs. Applying it to a coach with exactly 12 products is my inference (confidence: high, because the same rule shows up in three separate videos).

**How we get there**
1. His rule for anyone starting out: "you want to sell one product or service to one avatar on one channel until you make $1 million." ([jfW6gL6hKhk @ 8:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=489s))
2. He applies the same rule to product range: "if you give customers everything they want, they will create their own demise. Nobody wants a thing that has everything." ([XGm2ERU9qtA @ 22:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1344s))
3. A coach with 12 parallel products breaks the "one product" part of that rule twelve times over. Most likely they're also selling to several avatars, which breaks the "one avatar" part too.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Being spread thin:** "The price of wanting to be good at everything is being good at nothing." ([XGm2ERU9qtA @ 22:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1344s))
- **The likely cause:** "when people are afraid of making decisions, they say yes to everything because they're so afraid of saying no" ([XGm2ERU9qtA @ 22:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1378s))
- **Depth:** "you can't go deep if you have too many things" and "all of the outsized returns come on the end of the curve" ([-JLN1d1ZKUU @ 8:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=529s))
- **Resources:** working on two or three solutions at once "ends up just pulling resources from the one way that I know will work but will take time" ([-JLN1d1ZKUU @ 6:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=364s))
- **His test for cutting:** "how much can I take away and still have it be good and not only be good but it probably is better" ([-JLN1d1ZKUU @ 11:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=662s))
- **Effect on clients:** in his own community, "the number one reason that people were cancelling was overwhelm" ([-JLN1d1ZKUU @ 11:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=662s)). A catalogue of 12 products confuses buyers and overwhelms clients.
- **Over-extension:** "Businesses rarely die of starvation. They often die of indigestion." ([tGhe3sBuk34 @ 9:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=561s))

**What he's done:** He cut his Skool Games community from three calls a week to one and switched off app features because members were overwhelmed. At Gym Launch, the gym owners said the only thing they wanted was more leads. He also admits he has the opposite habit himself: he gets impatient after about 30 days and starts a second approach, which he calls a mistake.

**What would change his answer:** His idea of a "money model" isn't against selling more than one thing. He wants you to make more from each customer through upsells, like the "menu" upsell: you talk the customer out of what they don't need, then offer a choice between two options. That means selling one core offer first and adding other offers in sequence to the same customer. If the coach's 12 "products" are really one core offer plus upsells and downsells offered to the same avatar at the right moments, he'd be fine with it. He'd likely just cut it down to fewer. If it's 12 separate offers each fighting for attention, his answer is to cut them. He also makes an exception for enterprise businesses serving the Fortune 100, but that doesn't apply to a coach.
